q: A Monte Carlo estimate is best described as …
o: an exact answer from a formula
an average over random draws of a model
why: It estimates an expected value E[f(X)] by averaging f over many random draws of X.

q: Outcomes have SD σ = 2. What is the MCSE of their mean with N = 10,000 runs?
How many times more runs do you need to halve the Monte Carlo standard error?
why: Error falls like 1/√N, so halving it needs √N to double: 4× the runs.

q: How many times more runs give 10× more precision (one more correct digit)?
why: 10× smaller error needs √N to grow 10×, so N grows 100×.

q: 10,000 runs give MCSE 0.004. How many runs give MCSE 0.001?
A million runs guarantee an accurate answer.
why: Myth. Runs shrink only the sampling noise; a wrong model or wrong inputs give a precisely computed wrong answer.

q: The Monte Carlo error rate 1/√N does not depend on the number of uncertain inputs.
why: True: that is why simulation beats grids, whose cost grows exponentially with the number of inputs.

q: P(cost > budget) can be estimated by simulation because it equals …
o: E[1(cost > budget)], the mean of an indicator
the budget divided by the mean cost
why: A probability is the average of a 0/1 outcome, so it is an expected value like any other.

q: With MCSE 0.0052, how should an estimate of 3.13784 be reported?
why: Round to the error and give the interval: extra digits are noise.

q: Who suggested the name 'Monte Carlo' for the method at Los Alamos?
why: Metropolis named it after the Monte Carlo casino; Ulam conceived the method in 1946 and von Neumann planned it for ENIAC.
